Harrogate's population increased by around 4,800 between the last two censuses (held in 2011 and 2021). This semi-automated article highlights some of the most notable changes among the local population.

The population passed 160,000

Between the last two censuses (held in 2011 and 2021), the population of Harrogate increased by 3.0%, from just under 157,900 in 2011 to around 162,700 in 2021.

The population here increased by a smaller percentage than the overall population of Yorkshire and The Humber (3.7%), and by a smaller percentage than the overall population of England (up 6.6% since the 2011 Census).

In 2021, Harrogate was home to around 0.9 people per football pitch-sized piece of land. This area was among the lowest 10% for population density across English local authority areas at the last census.

This article generally uses percentages to enable comparisons over time and between areas. The percentage point change is also used to show the difference between the 2011 and 2021 percentages.

Population growth was lower in Harrogate than across Yorkshire and The Humber

An older Harrogate

Between the last two censuses, the average (median) age of Harrogate increased by four years, from 43 to 47 years of age.

This area had a higher average (median) age than Yorkshire and The Humber as a whole in 2021 (40 years) and a higher average (median) age than England (40 years).

The median age is the age of the person in the middle of the group, meaning that one half of the group is younger than that person and the other half is older.

The number of people aged 50 to 64 years rose by just over 4,900 (an increase of 15.5%), while the number of residents between 35 and 49 years fell by around 5,300 (15.1% decrease).

The share of residents aged between 50 and 64 years increased by 2.4 percentage points between 2011 and 2021

National identity in Harrogate

The percentage of people who did not identify with any national identity associated with the UK fell in Harrogate, but rose across Yorkshire and The Humber.

In Harrogate, the percentage that did not identify with any UK national identity fell from 5.8% in 2011 to 5.1% in 2021. During the same period, the regional percentage increased from 5.1% to 6.7%.

The percentage of people who identified with a UK and non-UK national identity in Harrogate increased from 0.5% to 1.4%, while the percentage of people who identified as "British only" increased from 17.1% to 60.0%.

In Census 2021, “British” was moved to the top response option and this may have influenced how people described their national identity. For further information, please see our quality report.

The percentage of people who did not identify with at least one UK national identity in Harrogate decreased by 0.7 percentage points

Harrogate stood out from other areas for housing

The percentage of households in the social rented sector increased here, but fell across Yorkshire and The Humber.

In Harrogate, the percentage of households in the social rented sector rose from 9.1% in 2011 to 9.9% in 2021. During the same period, the regional percentage fell from 18.1% to 17.3%.

Private renting in Harrogate increased from 17.5% to 19.0%, while the rate of home ownership decreased from 71.1% to 70.1%.

The rate of social renting in Harrogate increased by 0.7 percentage points

Harrogate residents' country of birth

In the latest census, around 142,000 Harrogate residents said they were born in England. This represented 87.3% of the local population. The figure has risen from around 137,500 in 2011, which at the time represented 87.1% of Harrogate's population.

Scotland was the next most represented, with just over 3,900 Harrogate residents reporting this country of birth (2.4%). This figure was down from just under 4,200 in 2011, which at the time represented 2.6% of the population of Harrogate.

The number of Harrogate residents born in Poland rose from around 1,400 in 2011 (0.9% of the local population) to around 1,600 in 2021 (1.0%).

In 2021, 87.3% of Harrogate residents reported their country of birth as England

Unpaid care in Harrogate

Harrogate saw Yorkshire and The Humber's joint second-largest percentage-point fall (alongside Hambleton and Ryedale) in the proportion of people (aged five years and over) providing up to 19 hours of weekly unpaid care (from 7.7% in 2011 to 4.7% in 2021). These are age-standardised proportions.

Age-standardised proportions are used throughout this section. They enable comparisons between populations over time and across geographies, as they account for differences in the population size and age structure.

Across the region, only Craven saw a greater fall in the proportion of people (aged five years and over) providing up to 19 hours of weekly unpaid care (from 8.4% to 5.0%).

Every local authority area across Yorkshire and The Humber saw a fall in the proportion of people (aged five years and over) providing up to 19 hours of weekly unpaid care, as the regional proportion fell from 7.1% to 4.4%.

Census 2021 was undertaken during the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic. This may have influenced how people perceived and managed their provision of unpaid care, and therefore may have affected how people chose to respond.

Caution should be taken when making comparisons between 2011 and 2021 because of changes in question wording and response options.

The percentage of people (aged five years and over) providing up to 19 hours of weekly unpaid care in Harrogate decreased by 3.0 percentage points

Unemployment in Harrogate

In 2021, 1.7% of Harrogate residents (aged 16 years and over) said they were unemployed. This figure decreased from 2.3% in 2011.

In 2021, just under 6 in 10 people (57.6%) said they were employed (excluding full-time students), compared with 61.5% in 2011. The percentage of retired Harrogate residents increased from 24.4% to 26.9%.

The decrease in the percentage of people aged 16 years and over (excluding full-time students) who were unemployed was greater across Yorkshire and The Humber (1.6 percentage points, from 4.4% to 2.7%) than in Harrogate (0.6 percentage points). Across England, the percentage fell by 1.1 percentage points, from 4.0% to 2.9%.

Census 2021 took place during the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic, a period of rapid and unparalleled change; the national lockdown, associated guidance and furlough measures will have affected the labour market and our ability to measure it.

The percentage of people aged 16 years and over who were unemployed (excluding full-time students) in Harrogate decreased by 0.6 percentage points

Fewer adults working long hours

Harrogate saw Yorkshire and The Humber's second-largest percentage-point fall in the proportion of people aged 16 years and over and in employment who said they usually worked over 49 hours per week (from 16.9% in 2011 to 13.4% in 2021).

Across the region, only Richmondshire saw a greater fall in the percentage of people aged 16 years and over and in employment who said they usually worked over 49 hours per week (from 26.4% to 17.8%).

Every local authority area across Yorkshire and The Humber saw a fall in the percentage of people aged 16 years and over and in employment who said they usually worked over 49 hours per week, as the regional percentage fell from 11.9% to 9.9%.

Working hours may have been affected by the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic.

The percentage of adults in employment who worked 49 hours or more in Harrogate decreased by 3.5 percentage points

Health in Harrogate

In 2021, 53.0% of Harrogate residents described their health as "very good", increasing from 50.9% in 2011. Those describing their health as "good" fell from 33.9% to 32.9%. These are age-standardised proportions.

Age-standardised proportions are used throughout this section. They enable comparisons between populations over time and across geographies, as they account for differences in the population size and age structure.

The proportion of Harrogate residents describing their health as "very bad" was 0.7% (similar to 2011), while those describing their health as "bad" was 2.7% (similar to 2011).

These data reflect people’s own opinions in describing their overall health on a five point scale, from very good to very bad.

Census 2021 was conducted during the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic. This may have influenced how people perceived and rated their health, and therefore may have affected how people chose to respond.

The percentage of people in good health in Harrogate decreased by 1.0 percentage points

Religion in Harrogate

In 2021, 36.2% of Harrogate residents reported having "No religion", up from 22.9% in 2011. The rise of 13.3 percentage points was the largest increase of all broad religious groups in Harrogate. Because the census question about religious affiliation is voluntary and has varying response rates, caution is needed when comparing figures between different areas or between censuses.

Across Yorkshire and The Humber, the percentage of residents who described themselves as having "No religion" increased from 25.9% to 39.4%, while across England the percentage increased from 24.8% to 36.7%.

In 2021, 55.5% of people in Harrogate described themselves as Christian (down from 68.6%), while 6.3% did not state their religion (down from 7.1% the decade before).

There are many factors that can cause changes to the religious profile of an area, such as a changing age structure or residents relocating for work or education. Changes may also be caused by differences in the way individuals chose to self-identify between censuses. Religious affiliation is the religion with which someone connects or identifies, rather than their beliefs or religious practice.

In 2021, 36.2% of usual residents in Harrogate reported having "No religion"

Family in Harrogate

In 2021, 5.8% of Harrogate households included a couple with only non-dependent children. This figure was at a similar level in 2011 (5.6%).

In 2021, just under one in five households (19.1%) included a couple with dependent children, compared with 21.0% in 2011. The percentage of single-family households including a couple without children decreased from 20.7% to 19.6%.

Harrogate saw Yorkshire and The Humber's joint third-largest rise (alongside Craven, Hambleton and Sheffield) in the percentage of households including a couple with only non-dependent children. This area had the region’s sixth lowest percentage of households including a couple with only non-dependent children.

The percentage of households including a couple with only non-dependent children in Harrogate increased by 0.2 percentage points

More adults never married or in a civil partnership

Of Harrogate residents aged 16 years and over, 29.8% said they had never been married or in a civil partnership in 2021, up from 27.0% in 2011.

In 2021, just over one in two people (51.3%) said they were married or in a registered civil partnership, compared with 53.7% in 2011. The percentage of adults in Harrogate that had divorced or dissolved a civil partnership increased from 9.5% to 10.0%.

The increase in the percentage of people aged 16 years and over who had never been married or in a civil partnership was greater across Yorkshire and The Humber (3.8 percentage points, from 33.9% to 37.7%) than in Harrogate (2.8 percentage points). Across England, the percentage increased by 3.3 percentage points, from 34.6% to 37.9%.

These figures include same-sex marriages and opposite-sex civil partnerships in 2021, neither of which were legally recognised in England and Wales in 2011. Same-sex marriages have been legally recognised in England and Wales since 2014 and opposite-sex civil partnerships have been recognised since 2019.

The percentage of adults who had never married or registered a civil partnership in Harrogate increased by 2.8 percentage points

Disability in Harrogate

In 2021, 5.4% of Harrogate residents were identified as being disabled and limited a lot. This figure decreased from 6.4% in 2011. These are age-standardised proportions.

Age-standardised proportions are used throughout this section. They enable comparisons between populations over time and across geographies, as they account for differences in the population size and age structure.

In 2021, just under 1 in 10 people (9.5%) were identified as being disabled and limited a little, compared with 8.8% in 2011. The proportion of Harrogate residents who were not disabled increased from 84.8% to 85.1%.

This area had the region’s lowest proportion of residents who were identified as being disabled and limited a lot. Craven had Yorkshire and The Humber's next lowest proportion of residents who were identified as being disabled and limited a lot (5.5%), while Barnsley had the region's highest proportion (10.6%).

Census 2021 was undertaken during the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic. This may have influenced how people perceived their health status and activity limitations, and therefore may have affected how people chose to respond.

Caution should be taken when making comparisons between 2011 and 2021 because of changes in question wording and response options.

The percentage of people who were identified as being disabled and limited a lot in Harrogate decreased by 1.0 percentage points

Ethnic groups in Harrogate

In 2021, 1.6% of Harrogate residents identified their ethnic group within the "Mixed or Multiple" category, up from 1.1% in 2011. The 0.5 percentage-point change was the largest increase among high-level ethnic groups in this area.

Across Yorkshire and The Humber, the percentage of people from "Mixed or Multiple ethnic groups" increased from 1.6% to 2.1%, while across England the percentage increased from 2.3% to 3.0%.

In 2021, 95.4% of people in Harrogate identified their ethnic group within the "White" category (compared with 96.3% in 2011), while 1.8% identified their ethnic group within the "Asian, Asian British or Asian Welsh" category (compared with 1.5% the previous decade).

The percentage of people who identified their ethnic group within the "Black, Black British, Black Welsh, Caribbean or African" category decreased from 0.7% in 2011 to 0.6% in 2021.

There are many factors that may be contributing to the changing ethnic composition of England and Wales, such as differing patterns of ageing, fertility, mortality, and migration. Changes may also be caused by differences in the way individuals chose to self-identify between censuses.
